say: It's nine p.m. A homeowner's water heater just burst. They call the first plumber on Google. Voicemail. They call the second. Voicemail again. The third one answers with a text in thirty seconds, and books the job.
The third plumber wasn't better. They were just automated.

In this video, I'll walk you through five real problems that cost small businesses money every single week, and exactly how to fix each one with AI. Real tools, real setup steps, and the mistakes to avoid.
Here's the plan. Missed leads. Slow follow-ups. Forgotten meetings. Late invoices. And content you never have time to post.
Problem one. Missed leads and the same ten questions, over and over.
Most small businesses can't answer the phone or the website chat while they're actually doing the work. So questions come in at night, on weekends, or in the middle of a job, and they sit there.
And here's the thing. Most of those questions are the same. What are your hours? Do you serve my area? How much does it cost? Can I book for Saturday?

v.title: Your inbox, every week
msgs: How much for a deep clean?

say: The fix is an AI assistant trained only on your business. It answers those questions instantly, twenty four seven, and when someone is ready to buy, it collects their details and hands them to you.

Tools that do this well include Tidio, Intercom's Fin, and Chatbase for your website, and ManyChat if most of your messages come through Instagram or Facebook. Most have free plans or free trials, so you can test before you pay.
Setup takes about an afternoon. First, write down your twenty most common questions and your real answers. Prices, hours, service areas, policies.

v.title: Setup in one afternoon
items: Write your top 20 questions + real answers

say: Second, paste that into the tool's knowledge base, along with your website pages.

v.title: Setup in one afternoon
items: Write your top 20 questions + real answers
Add them + your website to the knowledge base

say: Third, set a handoff rule. If someone wants to book, or asks something the bot doesn't know, it collects their name and number and notifies you right away.

v.title: Setup in one afternoon
items: Write your top 20 questions + real answers
Add them + your website to the knowledge base
Handoff rule: booking or unsure → collect details → notify you

say: And fourth, test it like an annoying customer. Ask it ten tricky questions before it goes live.

v.title: Setup in one afternoon
items: Write your top 20 questions + real answers
Add them + your website to the knowledge base
Handoff rule: booking or unsure → collect details → notify you

say: Here's what a good exchange looks like. A visitor asks, do you do same day repairs in Queens? The bot answers, yes, Monday to Saturday, if you book before noon. Want me to grab your details so the team can confirm a time? The visitor leaves their name and number, and you get a notification on your phone.

v.title: A good handoff
msgs: Yes! Mon–Sat if booked before noon.
Want me to grab your details?
Done ✓ The team will text you shortly.

say: The mistake to avoid: letting the bot guess. Tell it to answer only from your information, and to say, let me get a human for that, whenever it isn't sure. A wrong price quoted by a bot is worse than no answer at all.

v.title: Don't let it guess
v.text: Answer only from your info. Unsure? → "Let me get a human."

say: Problem two. Slow follow-ups.
Someone fills out your contact form. You see it three hours later, between jobs, and reply that evening. By then, they've already talked to two of your competitors.

Speed matters more than most owners think. A widely cited lead response study from MIT and InsideSales found that replying within five minutes, instead of thirty, made a lead about twenty one times more likely to become a real sales conversation.

v.label: more likely to qualify a lead when you reply in 5 minutes vs 30
v.source: Lead Response Management Study, MIT / InsideSales

say: The fix is a simple follow-up system. The form goes into a free CRM, like HubSpot. AI reads their message and drafts a personal reply that goes out in under a minute. You get a task to call them. And if they don't answer, a friendly check-in goes out on day three and day seven.

To connect the pieces, use Zapier or Make. Both let you build this without code. The trigger is new form submission. The actions are create contact, generate reply with AI, send email or text, and create task.

Here's the exact recipe. Step one, trigger: new form submission. Step two, create or update the contact in your CRM. Step three, send their message to AI with a prompt like, write a short, friendly reply to this inquiry, offer two time slots, sign it from me. Step four, send that reply by email or text. Step five, create a call task for you, and start the day three and day seven follow-ups.

v.title: The Zapier / Make recipe
items: Create or update contact in CRM
AI drafts a short, friendly reply with 2 time slots
Create call task + start Day 3 / Day 7 follow-ups

say: Here's what that first reply can look like. Hi Sarah, thanks for reaching out about the kitchen leak. We can come by tomorrow morning or Thursday afternoon. Which works better?

v.subject: Re: kitchen leak
body: Hi Sarah, thanks for reaching out about the kitchen leak.
We can come by tomorrow morning or Thursday afternoon.

say: It's specific to what they wrote, and it ends with an easy question. That's what gets replies.

The mistake to avoid: sequences that keep going after someone replies. Nothing feels more robotic than getting, just checking in, after you already booked. Always set the rule, stop the sequence when they reply.

v.title: Stop when they reply
v.text: Nothing says "robot" like a check-in after they already booked.

say: Problem three. Meetings where promises get lost.
You get on a call with a client. You promise a proposal by Friday, updated pricing, and a quick intro to your designer. Then three more calls happen, and one of those promises quietly disappears.
Writing good notes takes fifteen or twenty minutes per call, so most people just don't.

v.label: of note-writing per call, so most people skip it

say: The fix is an AI note taker. It joins your Zoom, Google Meet, or Teams call, records it, and sends you a summary with every action item a few minutes after you hang up.
Good options are Fathom, which has a generous free plan, Fireflies, Otter, or the AI features already built into Zoom and Google Meet.
The real power comes from the next step. Send those action items straight into wherever you already work. Your CRM, your task app, or even just your email. Now every promise has a due date.

v.title: Close the loop
nodes: Tasks in your CRM / to-do app
Every promise has a due date

say: So after a thirty minute sales call, instead of a blank page, you get something like this. Summary: client wants to relaunch their website before March. Action items: send proposal by Friday, share three pricing tiers, intro to the designer. Each one lands as a task with a date.

v.subject: Call summary: Acme Dental
body: Summary: wants website relaunch before March.

say: The mistake to avoid: recording without telling people. Always say the call is being recorded, and in some places it's a legal requirement that everyone agrees. A quick, mind if my AI note taker joins, works perfectly.

v.title: Always ask first
v.text: "Mind if my AI note taker joins?" Some places legally require consent.

say: Problem four. Chasing late invoices.
You did the work. The client is happy. And the invoice is thirty days overdue. Chasing it feels awkward, so you put it off, and meanwhile your cash flow takes the hit.

The fix is the easiest one in this video, because you probably already have it. QuickBooks, Xero, FreshBooks, Wave and Stripe all have automatic payment reminders. Most owners just never switch them on.

Set up three reminders. A friendly heads up three days before it's due. A reminder on the due date. And a firmer note seven days after. Every one should include a pay now link, so paying takes ten seconds.

And the wording matters. Something like, hi Mark, just a friendly reminder that invoice ten forty two is due on Friday. You can pay in a few seconds with the link below. Thanks again for the work together. Short, polite, and impossible to misread.

v.subject: Friendly reminder: invoice #1042
body: Hi Mark, just a friendly reminder that invoice #1042 is due Friday.
You can pay in seconds with the link below.

say: Two more upgrades make a big difference. Take a deposit up front for larger jobs. And offer card or bank payments on file for repeat clients, so they're charged automatically.

v.title: Get paid faster
items: 3 automatic reminders with a pay-now link
Card or bank on file for repeat clients

say: The mistake to avoid: an aggressive tone. These emails go out under your name. Keep them warm and simple, and pause reminders for clients you're already talking to about the bill.

v.title: Keep it warm
v.text: Reminders go out in your name. Friendly beats aggressive.

say: Problem five. No time to create content.
You know you should be posting. It builds trust, it brings in leads. But between running the business and serving clients, it's always the first thing to slip.
The fix is to create once, and let AI do the slicing. Once a week, record a ten minute voice memo answering one real question a customer asked you.

v.text: Record once. Let AI slice it.

say: Then AI turns that one recording into a blog post, a newsletter, three social posts, and short video clips. Claude or ChatGPT handle the writing, Descript or Opus Clip cut the videos, Canva handles graphics, and a scheduler like Metricool or Buffer posts it all for the week.
One honest hour a week becomes a full week of content.

v.label: a week becomes a full week of posts

say: Here's a prompt you can copy. Here is a transcript of me answering a customer question. Turn it into a LinkedIn post, an Instagram caption and a short newsletter. Keep my wording and examples, don't add facts I didn't say, and write like I talk.

v.subject: Copy this prompt
body: Here's a transcript of me answering a customer question.
Turn it into a LinkedIn post, an IG caption and a short newsletter.
Keep my wording and examples. Don't add facts I didn't say.

say: The mistake to avoid: generic AI content. If you just type, write a post about plumbing, you'll get the same bland post as everyone else. Feed it your own stories, your opinions and your real customer questions. That's what makes it sound like you.

v.title: Avoid generic AI content
v.text: Feed it YOUR stories, opinions and customer questions.

say: So where should you start? Not with all five.
For one week, write down every task that eats your time. Then pick the one that costs you the most, in hours or in lost money, and automate only that one this month.
A simple way to decide: for each task, multiply the hours it takes each week by what your time is worth, then add any money you lose from missed or late jobs. The biggest number wins.
Most businesses I see should start with follow-ups or missed leads, because those are directly tied to revenue. Get one system working, then add the next.
